<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Text message reminders (TMRs) and patient navigation (PN) increase bowel cancer screening uptake. To date, no studies have directly compared these interventions with one another.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a three-arm randomised controlled trial with individuals, in London, who had not completed bowel cancer screening within 18 weeks of invitation. Participants were randomised to receive no reminder (usual care), TMRs at 19, 21, 23 and 25 weeks, or a TMR at 19 weeks, with telephone PN at 21, 23 and 25 weeks. The primary outcome was participation within 26 weeks of invitation. Differences were assessed using logistic regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      On an intention-to-treat basis (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 3129), uptake was higher in the TMR and PN groups, compared with usual care (6.5% vs. 2.0%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001; 7.5% vs. 2.0%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). There was no significant difference between TMR and PN groups. In the per-protocol analysis (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 2294), uptake was significantly higher in the PN group than the TMR group (8.6 vs. 12.6%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.025). Subgroup analyses revealed telephone PN was significantly more effective than TMRs for men, specifically (14.5% vs. 6.7%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While TMRs are no more effective than PN in general, implementing PN could help reduce disparities in uptake between men and women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ISRCTN17245519.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Which is more effective at improving uptake of bowel cancer screening: text message reminders or patient navigation? Results from a three-arm RCT

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Clarifying the patterns of neural activation during fear extinction in anxiety disorders (ADs) is essential for advancing our understanding of inhibitory learning. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly characterized in large, heterogeneous cohorts of patients. Utilizing a delayed fear extinction fMRI paradigm, this study examined neural responses in 280 patients with ADs — comprising panic disorder, agoraphobia, panic disorder with agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, and multiple specific phobias — compared to 103 healthy controls (HC). The attenuation of neural activation to conditioned fear (CS+) and safety (CS−) stimuli from early versus late extinction was compared between groups. Subjective ratings of US-expectancy, arousal, and valence were also collected. In a whole-brain voxelwise analysis, patients showed significantly reduced attenuation of neural activation across both CS+ and CS− relative to HC from early compared to late phases of extinction learning. This pattern was observed in a broad network, encompassing the insular cortex (IC) and bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), among other regions. No interaction between group and stimulus type was observed. Region-of-interest analysis of the left anterior insular cortex confirmed that reduced attenuation in this region represents a robust neural signature of altered extinction learning in ADs. Furthermore, patients reported persistently higher fear expectancy and arousal than HC, consistent with sustained alterations in threat-related processing following extinction training. Together, these findings highlight altered extinction-related neural attenuation as a transdiagnostic feature of ADs, offering novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear extinction.</jats:p>
title: Reduced attenuation of neural activation during fear extinction learning in patients with anxiety disorders: a delayed fear extinction fMRI study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Posterior cortical impairments in visuospatial/perceptual function are common non-motor symptoms of the Lewy Body Dementias (LBD) and are relatively specific for LBDs compared to other dementias. Across populations, cognitive impairments correlate with the presence of α-synuclein (α-syn) pathology in limbic and neocortical brain regions. However, the specific role that α-syn pathology plays in driving cortical circuit dysfunction and cognitive impairment remains controversial. We hypothesized that inducing α-syn pathology in primary visual cortex (V1) in mice would impair neuronal activity and encoding of visual information, leading to visuoperceptual impairments. To test this, we injected α-syn pre-formed fibrils (PFF) into V1, causing the formation of sparse Lewy-like pathology. Using longitudinal in vivo two-photon (2P) calcium imaging over 6 months, we recorded visually evoked activity of pyramidal cells in layer 2/3 (L2/3) and quantified α-syn pathology using C05-05, a fluorescent ligand that binds aggregated α-syn. Measuring population activity, we found a greater percentage of neurons in PFF-injected mice were responsive to visual stimuli with lower direction selectivity compared to controls at 4–5 months post-injection (MPI). Neurons with somatic Lewy-like inclusions showed reduced activity compared to neighboring neurons without inclusions. Conversely, neurons without somatic inclusions showed increased activity, positively correlated with the local burden of α-syn pathology. Using a coherent motion discrimination task, we found no impairments in visuoperceptual ability in PFF-injected mice. Our results demonstrate that α-syn pathology leads to reductions in neuronal activity in cells with somatic inclusions and reciprocal changes in local population activity but does not impair visuoperceptual function. Reflecting the early stages of neocortical α-syn pathology, our model provides a framework for future studies to better understand the heterogeneity of cognitive symptoms and α-syn pathology across patients.</jats:p>
title: Cortical α-synuclein pathology induces neuronal hypoactivity and circuit changes but not functional impairments in a model of early Lewy body dementia

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Despite rising global rates for cocaine addiction, treatments options are limited. Psychological treatments remain the standard option but have only modest effectiveness. One major barrier to treatment success is that patients often make disadvantageous decisions that go against recovery, highlighting the need for strategies to support decision-making. Converging evidence indicates that decision-making deficits in cocaine addiction are driven by impaired processing of outcomes and risks. We investigated how patients with cocaine addiction use explicit outcomes and risk information to guide decision-making. One-hundred-and-five patients with moderate-to-severe cocaine use disorder (CUD) and 80 healthy control volunteers completed a decision-making task in which reward, loss, and probability information were provided explicitly. A subset of participants underwent diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts that underpin decision-making. We used generalized linear mixed-effects models to determine how rewards, losses, and probability influence decisions, and combined probabilistic tractography with principal component analysis to characterize the white matter tracts. We found that patients incorporated explicit probability information into their decisions to the same degree as control participants but showed reduced integration of outcomes. Notably, patients were less likely to integrate losses into their decisions than rewards. Although orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts did not differ between groups, individual variability predicted the extent to which reward and loss information guided decisions, irrespective of diagnosis. Overall, these findings reveal fundamental challenges in using outcomes, particularly negative ones, to guide decision-making in patients with CUD, emphasizing the need for additional support to promote adaptive choices during recovery.</jats:p>
title: Impaired outcome-based decision-making in human cocaine addiction
